title: Rebecca Gratz
hook: founded the first Jewish Sunday school in America in 1838

segments.voice: Yesterday, Grace Aguilar, and the line a woman's voice. Did you read a page by a woman writer? Today, one last woman for this stretch, a teacher across the ocean in Philadelphia. Day one thousand forty-four.

Sunday morning in Philadelphia. Church bells. Children in their best clothes walking to Sunday school with lesson books under their arms. And a few Jewish children watching them go, or walking along with their friends, because there is no Jewish school for them to go to. A woman named Rebecca Gratz notices, and asks herself a practical question. Why not a school for Jewish children, on the day they're free? In 1838, her answer gets its first class.
screen: `SUNDAY MORNING, PHILADELPHIA.` → `NO SCHOOL FOR JEWISH CHILDREN.` → `WHY NOT ONE OF OUR OWN?`

segments.voice: Rebecca Gratz was already busy. She came from a well-known Jewish family in Philadelphia, and she had spent years building things for people in need: a society to help orphans, a society of Jewish women to help poor Jewish families. She never married, and she helped raise her sister's children after their mother died. Then came the school. She called it the Hebrew Sunday School. The idea, a school on Sunday, was one her Christian neighbors were already using, and she saw no reason Jewish children couldn't have it too, filled with their own Bible, their own prayers, their own history. The teachers were young Jewish women, volunteers. They had few books, so they made do, and some of them wrote the lessons themselves. The children came. Behind it is a command the Torah gives to every parent, in the Shema itself: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thy house, and when thou walkest by the way." Rebecca Gratz took that and asked: and when the parents can't, who will? The school answered: the community will. And it would be women who taught. Her model, a Jewish school on the weekend, run by the community, spread to other cities, and versions of it still exist in synagogues today. There's also a story people tell, that she was the model for the Jewish heroine Rebecca in Walter Scott's novel Ivanhoe. Nobody has proven it. What can be shown is quieter: a woman, a free morning, and children who learned their own story.
screen: `ALREADY BUILDING FOR OTHERS.` · `A SCHOOL ON THE DAY THEY'RE FREE.` · `YOUNG WOMEN AS TEACHERS.` · `TEACH THEM DILIGENTLY.` · then, large: `SUNDAY SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: teach a child something. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a relative, a neighbor, a student. Think of one thing you know that they don't yet: how to tie a knot, a word in another language, a family story, a blessing, why the moon changes shape. Keep it small. Picture the moment you'll tell them, where you'll be sitting, what they'll ask. If you pray, you can hold that child in your prayer. If not, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Rebecca Gratz. The Philadelphia woman who built help for orphans and the poor, and opened the Hebrew Sunday School so Jewish children could learn their own story. Today's word.
Your line: sunday school. Today, teach a child one small thing, on whatever day you have free. Day one thousand forty-four.

howItsDone: Synagogues in America run weekend or after-school religious schools where volunteer and part-time teachers teach Hebrew, prayer, Bible, holidays and history, a model often traced to Rebecca Gratz's Hebrew Sunday School in Philadelphia.
